subtopic_detail: Classifying a perineal injury and choosing the setting for its repair
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite after a 27 year old woman in her first pregnancy has had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 3900 g baby following a second stage of 95 minutes. The midwife is concerned about the extent of the perineal injury and has asked you to examine it before any suturing.

With the woman consented and adequately analgesed, you find a tear through the vaginal mucosa and perineal body extending to the anal sphincter complex. On rectal examination the external anal sphincter is disrupted across less than half of its thickness, the internal anal sphincter is intact, and the anorectal mucosa is intact. Blood loss is 350 mL and she is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tear through vaginal mucosa and perineal body, external anal sphincter disrupted across less than half its thickness, internal anal sphincter intact, anorectal mucosa intact
data_table.Analgesia: Epidural sited in labour and still functioning

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the injury?

options.text: Repair in theatre under regional anaesthesia with antibiotic cover
options.rationale: Any disruption of the external anal sphincter is a third degree tear, and Australian practice is repair in an operating theatre with adequate regional or general anaesthesia, good lighting and assistance, together with a single dose of intravenous antibiotic (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Repair in the birth suite under local anaesthetic infiltration now
options.rationale: Birth suite repair under local anaesthesia is appropriate for first and second degree tears, and using it for a sphincter injury gives inadequate muscle relaxation and poorer identification of the retracted sphincter ends (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Leave unrepaired and review in the perineal clinic at six weeks
options.rationale: Delaying repair of a sphincter injury leads to retraction and fibrosis of the muscle ends and substantially higher rates of persisting faecal incontinence (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Refer to colorectal surgery for a delayed repair at six weeks
options.rationale: Secondary sphincter repair is reserved for injuries missed at birth or for failed primary repair, and it has poorer functional results than immediate repair (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

options.text: Perform a defunctioning colostomy before any perineal repair
options.rationale: A defunctioning stoma is considered only for extensive fourth degree injury with gross contamination, and it has no place in a partial thickness external sphincter tear with intact anorectal mucosa (Source: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury complicates around 3 per cent of vaginal births in Australia and around 6 per cent of first vaginal births, and the outcome depends heavily on recognition at the time. Classification is by depth: 3a is less than half the external sphincter thickness, 3b is more than half, 3c involves the internal sphincter as well, and a fourth degree tear breaches the anorectal mucosa. Every woman should have a systematic rectal examination after vaginal birth precisely because these tears are missed when only the perineum is inspected. Repair is followed by a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotic, a laxative regimen for ten days, physiotherapy referral and follow up at six to twelve weeks, with a discussion about mode of birth in a future pregnancy.
key_points: Perform a rectal examination after every vaginal birth to identify sphincter injury
3a involves less than half the external sphincter and 3b more than half
3c adds internal sphincter involvement and fourth degree breaches the anorectal mucosa
Repair sphincter injuries in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia
Follow repair with antibiotics, laxatives and physiotherapy referral
explanation.pearls: Prescribe a stool softener such as lactulose for ten days after sphincter repair and avoid constipating agents, because straining against a fresh repair is a recognised cause of breakdown and persisting incontinence.

sources.label: RANZCOG Third and Fourth Degree Perineal Tears
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Pathway after a high risk genotype is detected on a self collected screening sample
stem:
You are the general practitioner following up a 38 year old woman whose cervical screening was four years overdue. She declined a speculum examination because of a history of sexual assault, and at her last visit she collected a vaginal sample herself in the practice bathroom after you explained the technique.

The laboratory reports that oncogenic human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 have been detected, and notes that cytology cannot be performed on a self collected sample. She has never had an abnormal screening result before, has no abnormal bleeding and no pelvic pain, and is not pregnant.

data_table.Screening result: Self collected vaginal sample, oncogenic human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 detected, no cytology performed
data_table.History: Last cervical screening test negative six years ago, no previous abnormal result

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months time
options.rationale: A twelve month repeat is the pathway for oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 with negative or low grade cytology, and applying it here would delay diagnosis of a possible high grade lesion (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).

options.text: Refer directly for colposcopy at the local gynaecology service
options.rationale: Detection of types 16 or 18 on any sample, including a self collected one, requires direct referral for colposcopy regardless of cytology, because these genotypes account for around 70 per cent of cervical cancers (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange a clinician collected sample for reflex liquid based cytology
options.rationale: Cytology does not change the destination when types 16 or 18 are found, and requiring a speculum examination first adds a barrier for a woman who chose self collection for good reason (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).

options.text: Return to routine five yearly cervical screening as scheduled
options.rationale: Routine recall follows a negative human papillomavirus result, and returning a woman with a high risk genotype to five yearly screening misses the group at greatest risk of invasive disease (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and review the result in four weeks
options.rationale: Ultrasound does not visualise the transformation zone and has no role in the assessment of an abnormal screening result (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The renewed National Cervical Screening Program uses primary human papillomavirus testing every five years from 25 to 74 years of age, with partial genotyping that separates types 16 and 18 from the other oncogenic types. Self collection has been available to every screening participant since 2022 and performs equivalently to clinician collection for detecting the virus, which matters because under screened women account for most cervical cancers in Australia. The limitation is that cytology cannot be run on a self collected vaginal sample, so the management pathway is driven by genotype alone. Types 16 or 18 go straight to colposcopy, while other oncogenic types on a self collected sample lead to a clinician collected sample for cytology, or direct colposcopy if that is not acceptable to the woman.
key_points: Types 16 or 18 detected on any sample means direct colposcopy referral
Other oncogenic types on self collection lead to a clinician collected sample for cytology
Self collection performs equivalently to clinician collection for virus detection
Screening runs five yearly from 25 to 74 years of age
Under screened women account for the majority of cervical cancers in Australia
explanation.pearls: Types 16 and 18 cause about 70 per cent of cervical cancers, which is why their detection bypasses cytology triage entirely and sends the woman straight to colposcopy even when she has no symptoms and a normal examination.

subtopic_detail: Treating antiphospholipid syndrome in a new pregnancy after recurrent first trimester loss
stem:
You are the early pregnancy unit registrar seeing a 33 year old woman who is six weeks pregnant and has had three consecutive first trimester losses at seven, nine and eight weeks. She has no living children and describes the previous appointments as the hardest part of the past two years.

Investigations arranged between pregnancies showed normal parental karyotypes, a normal uterine cavity on three dimensional ultrasound, normal thyroid function and a normal glycated haemoglobin. Lupus anticoagulant was positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart, while anticardiolipin and anti beta 2 glycoprotein I antibodies were negative on both occasions. Today an ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with a foetal heart rate of 118 beats per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 218 x10^9/L (150-400), activated partial thromboplastin time prolonged and not correcting on mixing, full blood count and renal function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Single intrauterine gestational sac with a crown rump length consistent with six weeks and a visible foetal heart

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of this pregnancy?

options.text: Commence aspirin 100 mg daily alone from the first positive test
options.rationale: Aspirin alone is less effective than combined therapy in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome, and the addition of heparin is what improves the live birth rate in this group (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Commence prednisolone 10 mg daily with aspirin 100 mg daily now
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not improve live birth rates in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome and increase gestational diabetes, hypertension and preterm birth (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage).

options.text: Commence aspirin 100 mg daily with prophylactic dose enoxaparin
options.rationale: Persistent lupus anticoagulant with three consecutive losses before ten weeks meets the criteria for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome, treated with low dose aspirin plus prophylactic low molecular weight heparin started once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Commence therapeutic dose enoxaparin with aspirin 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Therapeutic dose anticoagulation is used when there has been a prior thrombotic event, and this woman has purely obstetric disease so the higher dose adds bleeding risk without benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Arrange intravenous immunoglobulin infusions each trimester now
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has not been shown to improve live birth rates in this condition and is not funded for this indication in Australia (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage).

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the only cause of recurrent miscarriage for which treatment reliably improves live birth rates, which is why it is sought in every recurrent miscarriage workup alongside parental karyotype, uterine imaging and thyroid and glycaemic assessment. Laboratory diagnosis requires lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti beta 2 glycoprotein I antibodies persisting on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, and lupus anticoagulant alone is sufficient if persistent. The obstetric clinical criteria are three or more consecutive losses before ten weeks, one or more losses of a morphologically normal foetus at or beyond ten weeks, or a birth before 34 weeks for severe preeclampsia or placental insufficiency. Combined aspirin and heparin raises live birth rates to around 70 to 80 per cent, and these pregnancies also need growth surveillance and preeclampsia vigilance in the second half.
key_points: Antibodies must persist on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart
Lupus anticoagulant alone is sufficient if persistently positive
Aspirin plus prophylactic heparin is the treatment for purely obstetric disease
Therapeutic dose heparin is reserved for prior thrombosis
Corticosteroids and immunoglobulin do not improve live birth rates
explanation.pearls: Start low dose aspirin before or at conception and add prophylactic enoxaparin once an intrauterine pregnancy with a foetal heart is confirmed on ultrasound, continuing the heparin until six weeks postpartum because thrombotic risk persists into the puerperium.

subtopic_detail: First line treatment of a scarring vulval dermatosis with malignant potential
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old woman with 18 months of vulval itching that is worst at night and now makes sex painful. She has tried three courses of antifungal cream bought from the pharmacy with no benefit.

There are white, thin, crinkled plaques over the labia minora, clitoral hood and perineum extending around the anus in a figure of eight pattern, with fusion of the skin over the clitoris and loss of the labia minora. There is no ulceration, no fixed lump and no thickened indurated area. The vaginal walls appear normal and a swab for microscopy and culture shows no candida.

data_table.Investigations: Vulvovaginal swab negative for candida and bacterial pathogens, fasting glucose and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Examination: White atrophic plaques in a figure of eight distribution with clitoral hood fusion and resorption of the labia minora, no ulceration or induration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Apply clotrimazole 1 per cent cream twice daily for four weeks
options.rationale: A further antifungal repeats a treatment that has already failed three times and does not address an inflammatory scarring dermatosis (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Skin Disorders).

options.text: Apply oestriol 0.01 per cent cream three nights a week ongoing
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary syndrome of menopause, and the near pair distinction is that the vaginal walls are normal here while the changes are confined to keratinised vulval skin (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Skin Disorders).

options.text: Refer for a vulval punch biopsy before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is required when the appearance is atypical, when there is an ulcer or thickened area, or when the condition fails to respond, and none of those apply to this classic presentation (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Skin Disorders).

options.text: Apply clobetasol propionate 0.05 per cent ointment nightly
options.rationale: An ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line for lichen sclerosus, relieving symptoms, halting architectural change and reducing the risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Skin Disorders; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for wide local excision of the affected vulval skin
options.rationale: Surgery has no role in uncomplicated lichen sclerosus, recurs in the surgical scar, and is reserved for malignancy or for division of adhesions causing functional problems after medical control (Source: RANZCOG Vulval Skin Disorders).

explanation.summary: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with a peak incidence after menopause, and it is repeatedly misdiagnosed as thrush because itch is the dominant symptom. The diagnosis is usually clinical, resting on white atrophic skin in a figure of eight distribution around the vulva and anus with loss of architecture, notably resorption of the labia minora and burying of the clitoris. Around 4 to 5 per cent of untreated women develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma, and there is good evidence that adherent topical corticosteroid treatment reduces that risk as well as controlling symptoms. Treatment is lifelong with a maintenance regimen after the initial induction course, and any persistent ulcer, fissure or thickened plaque during follow up is an indication for biopsy.
key_points: Itch that has failed repeated antifungal treatment should prompt reassessment
The figure of eight distribution and architectural loss are diagnostic clues
Ultrapotent topical corticosteroid is first line and is used long term
Around 4 to 5 per cent of untreated women develop vulval squamous cell carcinoma
Biopsy any ulcer, fissure or thickened plaque that appears during follow up
explanation.pearls: The usual Australian induction regimen is clobetasol propionate 0.05 per cent ointment nightly for four weeks, alternate nights for four weeks, then twice weekly for four weeks, followed by lifelong maintenance titrated to symptoms and examination findings.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic selection for group B streptococcal prophylaxis when the isolate and the patient both limit options
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 31 year old woman in her second pregnancy who is in established labour at 39 weeks and 2 days, contracting three times in ten minutes with the cervix 5 cm dilated. Her membranes ruptured two hours ago with clear liquor and she is afebrile.

Her combined vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus, and the laboratory has reported the isolate as resistant to both clindamycin and erythromycin. She tells you that as a teenager penicillin caused her face to swell and her throat to close over, and that she was given an adrenaline injection in the emergency department.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 140 beats per minute
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal and rectal swab at 36 weeks positive for group B streptococcus with resistance to clindamycin and erythromycin, full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Baseline 140 beats per minute with normal variability and no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Give intravenous cefazolin 2 g then 1 g every eight hours in labour
options.rationale: A cephalosporin is acceptable for a non severe penicillin allergy such as a delayed rash, but a history of angioedema with airway involvement requiring adrenaline is a severe immediate reaction where cross reactivity risk is unacceptable (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intravenous clindamycin 600 mg every eight hours in labour
options.rationale: Clindamycin is the alternative for severe penicillin allergy only when the isolate is susceptible, and this isolate has been reported as resistant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give intravenous erythromycin 500 mg every six hours in labour
options.rationale: Macrolides achieve poor and unreliable concentrations in foetal tissues and this isolate is resistant, so erythromycin is no longer recommended for this indication (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give no prophylaxis and observe the baby for 48 hours after birth
options.rationale: Withholding prophylaxis in a colonised woman leaves a risk of early onset neonatal sepsis of around one in 200, and observation does not prevent the disease it is watching for (Source: RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus).

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin as prophylaxis throughout the labour
options.rationale: With a severe immediate penicillin allergy and an isolate resistant to clindamycin, vancomycin is the recommended agent for intrapartum group B streptococcal prophylaxis in Australia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus).

explanation.summary: Early onset group B streptococcal disease remains the leading cause of neonatal sepsis in the first week of life, and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis reduces it by around 80 per cent when given for at least four hours before birth. Australian units use either universal screening with a combined vaginal and rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks or a risk factor based approach, and both require a clear antibiotic algorithm. Benzylpenicillin is first line, cefazolin is used for non severe penicillin allergy, and severe immediate allergy leads to clindamycin if the isolate is susceptible or vancomycin if it is not, which is why susceptibility testing is requested on every antenatal isolate from a woman reporting penicillin allergy. Documenting the nature of the reaction matters as much as the label itself, since most reported penicillin allergies are not immunoglobulin E mediated and unnecessarily divert women to inferior agents.
key_points: Prophylaxis is most effective when given at least four hours before birth
Benzylpenicillin is first line and cefazolin covers non severe allergy
Severe immediate allergy requires clindamycin only if the isolate is susceptible
Vancomycin is used when the isolate is clindamycin resistant
Request susceptibility testing on antenatal isolates from penicillin allergic women
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the penicillin reaction involved angioedema, breathing difficulty, hypotension or adrenaline, because that single question separates the women who can safely receive cefazolin from those who need vancomycin.
